title: Bridging Law Firm Silos: How Law Firms Can Maximize AI-Driven Cross-Selling (James Barclay, CEO Passle)
author: James Barclay

dom.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Barclay argues for legal-specific technology, but his evidence concerns law-firm thought leadership and marketing workflows. It does not address in-house AI adoption, selective insourcing, outside-counsel substitution, or corporate legal departments as stronger buyers, so his position relative to the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source contains only podcast closing remarks and provides no substantive claims, evidence or recommendations bearing on pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, transformation evidence or forecast workflows.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Barclay supports the cluster’s core claim that specialist legal software retains value through sector-specific design and workflow fit, explicitly rejecting generic products simply transplanted into legal. His evidence concerns a thought-leadership platform rather than generative-AI legal work, lawyer–engineer collaboration or verified copilot deployment, so it supports only the specialist-workflow portion of the synthesis.
qs: And if you're going to develop technology for Legal, you've got to develop it for Legal with them in mind.
You can't build something generic and then drop it in and hope for the best.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source supports the proposition with examples of technology-enabled content matching and a planned managed subpoena service intended to shift legwork away from legal teams. However, it provides no measured evidence that biography matching improves cross-selling, and the subpoena service is promotional and future-facing rather than demonstrated.
qs: So it's gone, it's taken the thought leadership, it's taken Alice's bio, and it's matched those two as well.
Basically, Percipient handles legwork so your team can focus on the core work.

kp.k: Cross-selling targets revenue lost through internal silos
kp.d: Barclay identifies awareness and trust as obstacles to cross-selling and reports Passle research asking managing partners to estimate foregone revenue: at least 10% was reportedly left on the table. No sample size or research methodology is supplied. He also relays a former Reed Smith CMO's characterization of cross-selling as the cheapest, fastest and easiest revenue-growth route, and a Latham's business-development director's hypothetical $10 billion rather than $6 billion firm. These are reported estimates and customer views, not demonstrated CrossPitch revenue gains.
qs: And one of the things we did was went off to managing partners and asked them what they thought they were leaving on the table as far as the money they weren't making because they weren't effectively cross-selling.
And the research that came back was at least 10% was left on the table.
he was saying, if only Latham's knew what Latham's knows, then we'd be a $10 billion firm instead of a $6 billion firm.

kp.k: Partnership responsibilities constrain lawyers' marketing capacity
kp.d: Barclay argues that legal technology must be designed specifically for law firms. His rationale is that lawyers simultaneously constitute the service product, own the business, and bear marketing and business-development responsibilities alongside annual hours demands. Passle's original thought-leadership platform addresses this time constraint through chief marketing and business-development officers rather than direct sales to individual lawyers.
qs: You can't build something generic and then drop it in and hope for the best.
And the thing about a lawyer is that they are the product, but they're also in charge of their own marketing, their own business development, their owners of the business.
And we don't sell directly to lawyers, we go to chief marketing officers, BD officers, and we're able to enable them to empower their attorneys to create thought leadership quickly and easily.

kp.k: AI matches published expertise to colleagues' potential interests
kp.d: Barclay describes CrossPitch as reading firm thought leadership and attorney biographies, then matching articles to colleagues likely to find them relevant and, by extension, their clients. Notifications identify the author, summarize the article in 80–100 words and explain relevance using the recipient's biography. This is AI-assisted internal expertise discovery and business development, rather than automation of substantive client legal work.
qs: It then goes and it reads all the bio pages of all the attorneys at your law firm.
It very specifically matches that piece of thought leadership with the attorneys who would be interested in that piece of thought leadership.
So it will say, hey, Alice, Oscar's written this post, and then it summarizes that post in 80 words to 100 words for Alice.
Importantly, in that e-mail, we also include a section that tells Alice specifically why she's received that e-mail.

kp.k: Automated distribution seeks relevance without notification overload
kp.d: Barclay says website thought leadership enters the system automatically, avoiding additional marketing-team work. Marketing and BD teams can adjust a relevancy meter and inspect why notifications were sent; he reports that a setting around 80 works well. His frequency descriptions differ: he states about two to three pieces per attorney per month, then one or two notifications per week. Both support his stated aim of limiting volume, but the transcript does not reconcile them.
qs: The whole thing runs in the background

kp.k: Technology supports trust but cannot resolve cross-selling alone
kp.d: Asked by Main about credit-sharing concerns and reluctance to expose clients to colleagues, Barclay explicitly rejects a silver-bullet claim. He proposes that repeated exposure to colleagues' expertise gradually builds trust and prompts human contact. An email-drafting feature, described as 'I saw this and thought of you,' reduces friction in sharing useful articles with clients; the lawyer still initiates and personalizes the communication.
qs: You're not suddenly going to launch CrossPitch and it's going to solve cross selling, right?
Second, third, fourth time, that's when the trust starts building up.
The likely thing she's going to do is reach out to him at the partner retreat or pick up the phone.
If they hit that, it will create an email for them.

kp.k: Reported engagement gains concern internal emails, not client conversion
kp.d: Main initially cites an increase from 18 percent to 42 percent and asks whether it concerns client sharing. Barclay clarifies that the metric is internal notification opens, reporting a current 44 percent rate that he says is increasing. He cites an 18 percent industry average and anecdotal five percent rates from unnamed Am Law 200 firms. No measurement period, sample size or conversion-to-revenue results are provided.
qs: What we can track is the open rates internally of these notifications.
The industry average 18 percent.
What we've seen is that the open rate on these CrossPitch notifications is 44 percent.
It's the internal open rate, which is unbelievably low with other notifications.

kp.k: Public-data scope supports intended rapid implementation
kp.d: Barclay says the product was deliberately scoped to public biographies and published thought leadership so it could be implemented within a week rather than require an initial four-month discussion with technology and risk functions. This is his implementation strategy and claim, not a documented comparison of deployment times.
qs: we wanted to build an AI tool that can be implemented within a week.
That requires us only to take public information.
The public information is the bios, which are obviously published, and the thought leadership, which is obviously published.

kp.k: Intelligence maps visualize potential collaboration and managerial leading indicators
kp.d: Barclay describes a map whose attorney nodes scale with thought-leadership production and whose links show distribution and opens, viewable by city, practice, industry and individual. He proposes using snapshots to identify active or inactive offices, practices and lateral hires, and to guide colleague outreach. He reports one unnamed Am Law 200 client asking lawyers to contact at least one, preferably two, colleagues weekly. The map is presented as a leading indicator of opportunities, not proof of completed cross-selling or revenue; Main separately suggests broader value as an indicator of contribution to the firm.
qs: The bigger the dot, the more thought leadership they've created. Then the lines are who that thought leadership has gone to.
It's indicative of the collaboration and the cross-selling opportunities within a law firm.
So you can then map that by city, by practice, by industry, and by individual.
One of the things one of our Am Law 200 clients is doing is that they are asking their lawyers every single week to connect with at least one, hopefully two other lawyers at the firm in some way.
You can start seeing how this is a leading indicator that drives behavior that drives cross-selling.

kp.k: Natural-language search extends internal expertise discovery
kp.d: Barclay describes CrossPitch Search as a complementary route to finding colleagues through natural-language requests and biographies, including interpreting geography. He contrasts it with an anecdotal test of a large firm's existing search: 'lawyer' returned 15 results despite thousands of lawyers, and a more specific M&A query returned none. His example illustrates claimed search functionality rather than a systematic accuracy evaluation.
qs: The flip side of that coin is search, because we now have an awesome search tool based on natural language and on bios.
I then put in M&A lawyer for a SaaS firm in Maryland. Zero came up, because it's all based on keywords and the name of the lawyer.
I've got a SaaS firm that I'm interested in selling, who could I talk to on the East Coast? And it will understand that and bring up New York, DC, Boston lawyers.

kp.k: Development favors narrow, iterative, client-shaped AI adoption
kp.d: Barclay reports that CrossPitch originated as an idea in January, launched in June and had 30 clients at interview time. Although the document is labeled 2026, the discussion refers to 2025 and a map release hoped for by Christmas; it does not unambiguously date these milestones. He advocates solving a bounded immediate problem and expanding through client feedback, using the IKEA effect as an analogy for client participation. Search and deeper adoption within clients are identified as development priorities.
qs: we only came up with this in January as an idea. We launched in June and we've now got 30 clients who are doing it.
The map is just coming out live in the next, hopefully by Christmas, and so we're running that with our clients.
That search function, I think, is probably is the big thing.
how do we work with our clients to build what we've got, to fit what they need?
you want to do something that solves the problem now. And then you can then see the next step of what you need to solve.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Barclay claims AI can support law-firm cross-selling by matching published expertise to relevant colleagues and gradually building awareness and trust.
pts.d: James Barclay, CEO of legal-tech vendor Passle, describes CrossPitch as reading attorneys' published thought leadership and biographies, matching content to colleagues, and sending targeted notifications with an 80–100-word summary and an explanation of relevance. He presents repeated exposure as a way to build trust and prompt internal conversations, rather than as an automatic solution to cross-selling. A built-in email-drafting feature also helps lawyers share colleagues' work with clients and prospects. The claimed change is augmentation of marketing and relationship development, not substitution for legal advice. Barclay links this opportunity to Passle's research suggesting at least 10% in foregone revenue; he does not claim demonstrated recovery of that amount through AI.

pts.k: Barclay claims targeted AI notifications achieve higher internal email engagement than ordinary internal communications.
pts.d: Barclay reports a 44% internal open rate for CrossPitch notifications, which he says is increasing, against an asserted 18% industry average and anecdotal reports of 5% from unnamed AmLaw 200 firms. These figures concern lawyers opening internal notifications, not clients opening forwarded articles or measured revenue conversion. He interprets the rising rate as indicating usefulness and anticipation among recipients.

pts.k: Barclay claims AI-linked visualisation makes potential collaboration and cross-selling activity visible and actionable.
pts.d: The Cross Selling Intelligence Map displays attorneys, content production, distribution connections and opens, organised by city, practice, industry or individual. Barclay presents these as leading indicators that can guide management attention, lateral integration and lawyers' decisions about whom to contact internally. The claim concerns visibility of potential connections and behaviour before revenue materialises; the source provides no demonstrated relationship between map activity and realised cross-selling revenue.

pts.k: Barclay claims natural-language search improves discovery of relevant lawyers, while public-data-only implementation allows rapid deployment.
pts.d: Barclay describes CrossPitch Search as interpreting a business need and geography against lawyer biographies rather than relying on exact keywords or names. His example is finding East Coast lawyers for the sale of a SaaS firm. He also says CrossPitch can be implemented within a week because it uses public biographies and thought leadership, and that automated ingestion and notification delivery avoid adding routine work for marketing teams. These are product-capability and deployment claims, not independent search-performance or implementation findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of vendor research, internal engagement metrics, product descriptions and client anecdotes, rather than measured cross-selling outcomes.
pts.d: Barclay says Passle asked managing partners to estimate revenue missed through ineffective cross-selling and obtained an 'at least 10%' estimate; no sample size, methodology or accounting basis is supplied. The 44% open rate is a vendor-reported observation without a measurement period, sample size or comparison design. His other support includes client consultations identifying cross-selling as a recurring concern, feedback at a Barnes and Thornburg partner retreat, an unnamed client's weekly internal-contact initiative, and his own example of poor keyword-search results at a large firm. He reports 30 CrossPitch clients following launch, which establishes claimed uptake rather than business impact. His reference to an Economist figure on AI project failures is an approximate secondary attribution, not evidence specifically evaluating CrossPitch.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Barclay presents deployment as near-immediate but relationship and revenue effects as gradual and dependent on human action.
pts.d: Barclay says the idea originated in January, launch occurred in June, and the map was expected to go live by Christmas. The document is labelled 2026 but the conversation refers to 2025 and does not clearly identify the year of these milestones. Search is described both as built and as an important development focus. Claimed one-week implementation relies on public content and biographies. Notifications depend on relevance settings, with approximately 80 described as a useful setting, and trust is expected to emerge after repeated exposure rather than the first message. Lawyers still need to contact colleagues or share content with clients. Reported notification frequency is internally inconsistent: Barclay mentions two to three pieces per month and then one or two notifications per week. No deadline or quantified forecast is given for revenue improvement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law-firm lawyers, marketing and business-development teams, firm leaders, and existing clients and prospects.
pts.d: Barclay focuses especially on US law firms, including AmLaw 200 firms with dispersed offices and practice groups, while also mentioning smaller firms. Lawyers receive relevant expertise, discover colleagues and obtain drafts for client outreach. CMOs and business-development officers buy and configure the tool, with automation intended to limit added workload. Managing partners gain visibility into content-sharing activity across offices, practices and lateral hires. Clients and prospects may receive more useful contact between engagements and introductions to additional expertise. Passle is the software vendor, not an ALSP delivering legal work. The source does not predict lawyer displacement, changes in staffing leverage, lower legal fees or improved access to justice.
